w: Construction began AD 72 under Vespasian, finished AD 80 under Titus, the largest amphitheatre ever built, holding an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators, averaging around 65,000, for gladiatorial contests, animal hunts, executions and mock sea battles before entertainment use ended in the medieval era.
s: Largest ancient amphitheatre, opened AD 80 under Titus
_facts: Built AD 72-80 under Vespasian and Titus
Used for gladiatorial contests, animal hunts, mock naval battles

w: Opened in 1877 and used by London Athletic Club until 1905, when new owner Gus Mears founded Chelsea FC to occupy it. Capacity is 40,044, the twelfth largest football ground in England. Record attendance 82,905 for Chelsea v Arsenal on 12 October 1935. Also hosted cricket, rugby, speedway and greyhound racing.
s: Chelsea's home since 1877, 12th largest in England

w: Home of Tottenham Hotspur from 1899 to 2017, hosting 2,533 competitive Spurs games across 118 years plus England internationals. Capacity fell from near 80,000 to an all-seated 36,284; record attendance 75,038 for an FA Cup tie v Sunderland, 5 March 1938. Demolished after the 2016-17 season.
s: Spurs' home 1899-2017, demolished for new ground

w: Built 1990-1992 in Copenhagen's Indre Osterbro district, home of FC Copenhagen and the Denmark national team, with a retractable roof and 38,190 capacity for football, expanding to 50,000-55,000 for concerts. Hosted three UEFA Euro 2020 group games plus a round of 16 match.
s: FC Copenhagen's retractable-roof home, Euro 2020
_facts: Home of FC Copenhagen and Denmark national team

w: Opened 20 May 1923, home of Valencia CF with 49,430 seats, the 8th largest stadium in Spain and largest in the Valencian Community. Named for the historic Mestalla irrigation canal that once ran past the south stand. Reckoned Europe's steepest ground, top tier reaching 34-35 degrees, and hosted 1982 World Cup matches.
s: Valencia CF's home since 1923, Europe's steepest

w: Completed in 1937 in Rotterdam's Feijenoord district, officially Stadion Feijenoord and nicknamed De Kuip, the Tub. Original capacity of 64,000 was expanded to 69,000 in 1949 then converted to a 51,117-seat all-seater in 1994. Home of Feyenoord and the Dutch national team, and a touring-concert venue until 2025.
s: Feyenoord's home since 1937, nicknamed The Tub

w: Home of Leeds United since the club's 1919 formation, with a 37,645 all-seated capacity across four stands including the Don Revie North Stand kop. Record league attendance 56,796 v Arsenal, 27 December 1932; record overall 57,892, an FA Cup fifth round replay v Sunderland, 15 March 1967. Hosted Euro 96 matches.
s: Leeds United's home since 1919, Euro 96 venue

w: The largest multi-purpose stadium in Toulouse, France, on the island of Ramier near the city centre, holding 33,150. Home mainly to Toulouse Football Club and Stade Toulousain rugby in the Top 14 and European Rugby Champions Cup. A dedicated football and rugby pitch with no surrounding athletics track.
s: Toulouse's biggest stadium, football and rugby
_facts: Home of Toulouse FC (football) and Stade Toulousain (rugby)

w: A football stadium in Leverkusen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, that has served as the home ground of Bundesliga club Bayer 04 Leverkusen since 1958, giving the club a permanent base near the Bayer chemical works that founded and still names the team and its arena.
s: Bayer Leverkusen's home ground since 1958

w: Home of the Rugby Football Union and England's national rugby union team, and the world's largest rugby union stadium, capacity around 82,000, second largest in the UK behind Wembley and fourth largest in Europe. Hosted NFL London Games in 2016 and 2017 and concerts by acts including the Rolling Stones and Beyonce.
s: World's largest rugby union stadium, England's home
_facts: Home of England national rugby union team

w: Home of FC Nantes, the Canaries, built in a hexagon shape and finished in 1984 for the European Football Championship, then renovated for the 1998 World Cup. Hosted rugby union group games at both the 2007 and 2023 Rugby World Cups in France plus men's and women's football at the 2024 Paris Olympics.
s: FC Nantes' hexagonal home, built for Euro 1984
_facts: Hosted 2007 and 2023 Rugby World Cup matches

w: Also known as Estadi Cornella-El Prat, opened August 2009 after three years of construction costing around 60 million euros, on the outskirts of Cornella de Llobregat and El Prat de Llobregat. Home of RCD Espanyol since 2009 with 40,500 seats, the tenth largest stadium in Spain, and a potential 2030 World Cup venue.
s: RCD Espanyol's home since 2009, opened for 60m euros

w: Opened April 1997 as a multi-functional indoor arena in Helsinki, home of ice hockey club Jokerit, seating 13,349 for hockey, around 14,000 for basketball and up to 15,000 for concerts. Formerly Hartwall Arena, it closed in 2022 under Russian ownership amid EU sanctions before reopening in 2025 as Veikkaus Arena.
s: Helsinki arena for Jokerit, reopened 2025

w: A cycling stadium in the Bois de Vincennes on the eastern edge of Paris, officially named Velodrome Jacques Anquetil - La Cipale after the French cycling great, and still known locally simply as La Cipale among Parisian track cyclists and cycling clubs that train and race there.
s: Paris cycling track in the Bois de Vincennes
_facts: Cycling stadium in the Bois de Vincennes, Paris
Officially named Velodrome Jacques Anquetil - La Cipale

w: Home of Manchester City from 1923 to 2003 in Moss Side, hosting FA Cup semi-finals, a League Cup final, Charity Shields and England matches. Record attendance 84,569 at an FA Cup sixth round tie v Stoke City in 1934, an English club ground record. Closed as a 35,150 all-seater when City moved grounds in 2003.
s: Man City's home 1923-2003, 84,569 record crowd

w: An indoor arena in Riga, Latvia, opened 15 February 2006 as Arena Riga for the 2006 IIHF World Championship, holding up to 14,500 for ice hockey, basketball and concerts. Designed by Canadian firm Stadium Consultants International with Latvian partners; renamed Xiaomi Arena in 2025 under a naming rights deal.
s: Riga's indoor arena, built for 2006 Worlds

w: Built in 1995 as the home ground of Granada CF, the city's main football club, in Granada, Spain. Used mostly for football, the multi-use stadium has a capacity of 21,600, making it one of the larger grounds in Andalusia outside the top La Liga giants.
s: Granada CF's home since 1995, 21,600 capacity

w: Formerly the People's Stadium, Nepstadion, in Budapest's 14th district Zuglo, a multi-purpose venue used mainly for football with an original capacity exceeding 100,000, reduced to a safe all-seated 38,652 by the 2000s. Closed in 2016 and demolished in 2017 to make way for the Puskas Arena on the same site.
s: Budapest's ex-Nepstadion, demolished 2017
_facts: Multi-purpose stadium in Budapest's Zuglo district

w: A multi-purpose indoor arena in Lisbon built in 1998 for the Expo '98 world's fair, formerly known as Pavilhao Atlantico and later Altice Arena. With a capacity of 20,000 it ranks among the largest indoor arenas in Europe and the largest in Portugal, hosting concerts and major indoor sporting events.
s: Lisbon's biggest indoor arena, built for Expo '98

w: A former football stadium in Dolmabahce, Istanbul, home ground of Besiktas and previously shared with Galatasaray and Fenerbahce. The all-seater held 32,145 spectators before being demolished, aside from the historic Eski Acik stand walls, for a new Besiktas stadium on the same site.
s: Besiktas' former home near Dolmabahce Palace
_facts: Former home of Besiktas football club
Demolished for a new Besiktas stadium

w: An indoor sport-concert complex in the center of Kyiv, Ukraine, run as an independent state enterprise. It stages a mix of sporting events and concerts and stands as one of the Ukrainian capital's principal indoor arenas, close to the historic core of the city.
s: Kyiv's indoor sport-concert complex, state-run
_facts: Indoor sport-concert complex in central Kyiv

w: Home of Scottish Premiership club Hibernian since the club first played there in 1893, with an all-seated capacity of 20,421, the fifth largest football ground in Scotland. Known to fans as The Holy Ground. Holds the record attendance for a Scottish match outside Glasgow, 65,860, at a 2 January 1950 Edinburgh derby.
s: Hibernian's home since 1893, The Holy Ground

w: An indoor stadium in Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy, whose Italian name translates as Olympic Ice Stadium, reflecting the Dolomite resort town's long history as a venue for Winter Olympic ice sports and international skating and hockey events.
s: Cortina's indoor Olympic ice stadium
_facts: Indoor ice stadium in Cortina d'Ampezzo, Italy

w: Also known as Stadio Giorgio Ascarelli, completed in 1929 in Naples with room for around 20,000, then rebuilt five years later with an upgraded capacity of 40,000. Home of SSC Napoli before the stadium was destroyed in 1942 during the Allied bombing of Naples in the Second World War.
s: Napoli's home 1929-1942, destroyed in WWII bombing
_facts: Destroyed in 1942 WWII bombing of Naples

w: Opened July 2012 as the home of Rotherham United, known as the AESSEAL New York Stadium for sponsorship, with a capacity of 12,021. Named after the New York district built around the Guest and Chrimes brass foundry, maker of fire hydrant stop taps once exported worldwide. Hosted matches at UEFA Women's Euro 2022.
s: Rotherham United's home since 2012

w: Completed 31 December 2003 and opened 31 March 2004 in Heraklion, Crete, seating 26,240. Used for football at the 2004 Athens Olympics tournament, it is home to Ergotelis and, from the 2025-26 season, OFI, plus occasional Greece national team fixtures.
s: Heraklion's stadium, 2004 Olympic football venue

w: Home of Wrexham AFC in Wales, the largest stadium in North Wales and seventh largest in Wales, holding 13,341. The world's oldest international football stadium still in international use, hosting Wales' first home international in 1877 and more Wales fixtures than any other ground.
s: Wrexham AFC's home, oldest international ground
_facts: World's oldest international football stadium in continuous use

w: The largest of Rome's gladiatorial schools, built by Emperor Domitian in the late first century AD just east of the Colosseum, between the Esquiline and Caelian hills. Gladiators from across the empire lived, ate and trained here before fighting at the Colosseum's games. Rebuilt under Trajan around AD 98-117.
s: Rome's gladiator training school by the Colosseum
_facts: Largest gladiatorial training school in ancient Rome
Built under Emperor Domitian, late 1st century AD
Located just east of the Colosseum

w: A multi-purpose stadium in Fez, Morocco, built in 2003 with athletics facilities and an original capacity of 45,000, currently holding about 35,468 after renovation. Set to host matches at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and the 2030 FIFA World Cup, with plans to expand seating to 55,800 by 2028.
s: Fez's stadium for 2025 AFCON and 2030 World Cup
_facts: Host venue for 2025 Africa Cup of Nations and 2030 World Cup

w: An indoor arena in the Miribilla neighbourhood of Bilbao, Spain, whose central hall holds up to 10,014 people for basketball games as well as concerts and other shows. The complex also includes swimming pools and gymnasiums used by local residents.
s: Bilbao's indoor arena in Miribilla

w: Built for Bury FC in 1885, one of the world's oldest professional football grounds. Capacity was 11,840 when last used in 2019 before Bury's expulsion from the English Football League; record attendance 35,000, a 1960 FA Cup tie. Fans bought the ground in 2022; Bury FC returned 2023.
s: Bury FC's home since 1885, saved by fans in 2022
_facts: Reopened by fan-owned Bury FC in 2023

w: Home ground of Como 1907 in Como, Italy, completed in 1927 on the orders of Benito Mussolini and designed by architect Giovanni Greppi, one of Italy's first rationalist-architecture buildings. Named for rower and First World War hero Giuseppe Sinigaglia, a Como native; capacity is 13,602.
s: Como 1907's home, built 1927 under Mussolini
_facts: Named for rower/WWI hero Giuseppe Sinigaglia

w: A multi-purpose stadium in Bucharest, Romania, used mainly for football and the home ground of Dinamo Bucuresti from the club's inception until 2022, when it failed to receive a hosting licence from Liga I and Liga II authorities. Its capacity stands at 15,032.
s: Dinamo Bucuresti's former home ground

w: A stadium in Baraki, a suburb of Algiers, Algeria, built at a cost of around 300 million euros with 40,784 seats, Algeria's first association-football-specific ground built without an athletics track and eligible to host FIFA World Cup matches. The 68-hectare complex includes a 6,000-vehicle car park and a heliport.
s: Algiers' 40,784-seat stadium, cost 300m euros
_facts: Located in Baraki, suburb of Algiers

w: The oldest stadium in Ljubljana, Slovenia, designed by architect Joze Plecnik and built from 1925 for the Catholic youth sport association Orel in the Bezigrad district. After the Second World War it became a football venue, home of NK Olimpija Ljubljana until the club's 2005 dissolution, and closed since 2008.
s: Ljubljana's oldest stadium, closed since 2008
_facts: Home of NK Olimpija Ljubljana until 2005

w: A football stadium in the Vozdovac district of Belgrade, Serbia, commercially named Stadion Shopping Center, and the home ground of FK Vozdovac. Opened in August 2013 atop a shopping mall, it is one of only a few rooftop stadiums in the world built for professional football, with a capacity of 5,200.
s: FK Vozdovac's rooftop stadium, opened 2013
_facts: Built atop a shopping mall, opened 2013
One of few rooftop professional football stadiums

w: A multi-purpose stadium in the Slavia district of Sofia, Bulgaria, home ground of PFC Slavia Sofia with a seating capacity of 25,000, among Bulgaria's biggest sports facilities. Part of a complex with training pitches and an ice hockey arena. Renamed for club legend Aleksandar Shalamanov after his death, October 2021.
s: PFC Slavia Sofia's home, 25,000 capacity
_facts: Renamed for club legend Aleksandar Shalamanov, 2021

w: Finland's first football stadium, built in 1915 in Helsinki's Toolo district and known by the nickname Bollis, now holding 4,000 spectators after a 2000-2001 renovation. Home to Atlantis FC and HJK Helsinki's women's team, it hosted five matches at the 1952 Helsinki Summer Olympics, including Germany v Brazil.
s: Finland's first football stadium, built 1915
_facts: Hosted five matches at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics

w: An arena and hotel complex in the Oliwa district of Gdansk, Poland, close to the Olivia Centre and the University of Gdansk's main campus. Owned by ice hockey club Stoczniowiec Gdansk and serving as its main venue for home games and related events.
s: Gdansk arena and hotel, Stoczniowiec's home
_facts: Home venue of ice hockey club Stoczniowiec Gdansk
